name: The Marknoble household — a name the town's own records carry

division_reconstructed.note: No source places this household anywhere — the record gives a name and no address, no street and not even a division. So BOTH halves of this band are dealt rather than read: the south division from the reconstruction order book's own household target by division, and the class from the town model's employment distribution, which puts this household under the placement policy's farms_and_country_seats clause. The places held before the plat stay where they were held: Beaubien's on the lakefront reservation, Clybourn's on the North Branch, Robinson and Caldwell's on the west ground. They are not seated by any of this — they are the reason the policy has to say 'outside the plat' at all. The deal is seeded on this household's own id, so it is the same on every run — and it is the weakest seat this ladder makes: no lot, no roof, no coordinate and no source behind either half of it.

printed_wife.printed: MARRIED, In this town, on Saturday evening 29 ult., by the Hon. R. I. Hamilton, Mr. MARK NOBLE, jun., second son of Mark Nobles, Esq. of this place, to Miss CHARLOTTE, only daughter of Mr. Charles Wesencraft, late of Buffalo.
printed_wife.what_happened: THE WIFE IS PRINTED, SO SHE IS NOT DRAWN. The paper marries them on 1833-11-29, before the scene date, and the town already held Charlotte Wesencraft on a card of her own, minted off the same column. She is seated here as his wife and that card is folded into this house; the wife the household model drew for it is not seated, and she is counted in the order book's cell for a woman of her band in his division, as a drawn wife would be. The house's size and its children are the model's, drawn by the same seeds as before and still the town's invention at the `reconstructed` tier: the paper names a marriage, not a family. It does not say where they lived, or that she was in Chicago on 1 July 1835; she stands in his house because a wife of nineteen months keeps her husband's house, and that is the reconstruction, not the source.

kin.note: THE NOTICE NAMES THE FATHER, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IS CLAIMED. The Chicago Democrat of 3 December 1833, column 7: 'Mr. MARK NOBLE, jun., second son of Mark Nobles, Esq. of this place'. Both cards were minted from that same reading of that same notice — the press register reads 'Mark Nobles, Esq.' and 'Mark Noble, Esq.', two lines apart, as the one father of the bridegroom and of the second bride — so nothing is being identified by name here. Written by T-2229, the family pass's ruling on this column (data/research/family_pass_rulings.json, chicago_democrat_1833_12_03 c007). The term 'son' is the paper's word, read off the notice and not off the card, whose sex is still a draw (T-2230 reads the column's 'Mr.' onto it). 'Second son' implies a first son, who is nobody this town holds, so no row is written for him. The marriage the same line prints is T-2230's to seat.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('marknoble_jun:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: THE NAME IS PRINTED WITH A TITLE, in the column and not on the name list. The paper prints 'Mr. MARK NOBLE, jun.' (chicago_democrat_1833_12_03#c007), and whoever set that line said in the same breath that this person was male. The press register files the person under the bare name, which is why rule 1 could not read it there; the title is read here where it was printed. A title is a statement about the person, and no draw stands against it.
